item.title: [Agriculture 101 #5] A Corn Plant Drinks Like a Firehose — And Keeps Almost None of It
item.body:
> Crops move enormous amounts of water from soil to air, and irrigation is really just the job of keeping that pipeline from running dry — without drowning the roots.

## Today's Concept

Here's a fact that surprises most people: a plant uses less than 1% of the water it absorbs to actually build itself. The other 99%-plus passes straight through and evaporates out of its leaves.

That process is called **transpiration**, and it isn't waste. It's the price of eating.

Leaves are covered in microscopic adjustable pores called **stomata**. A plant has to open them to let carbon dioxide in — CO2 is the raw material for photosynthesis, the sugar-making reaction that becomes grain, fruit, and fiber. But the inside of a leaf is a wet surface, and the air outside is usually drier. The instant those pores open, water vapor rushes out. There's no way to inhale CO2 without exhaling water. Farmers sometimes call this the plant's "carbon-for-water trade."

The escaping vapor pulls a continuous thread of water up from the roots. Water molecules cling to each other (cohesion) and to the walls of the plant's narrow plumbing, the **xylem**. So evaporation at the top literally drags the column upward — no pump, no heart, just tension. A tall corn plant on a hot July day in Iowa can move two to four liters through this straw.

The dryness of the air sets the pull rate. That's **vapor pressure deficit** (VPD) — the gap between how much moisture the air is holding and how much it could hold. Hot, dry, windy days mean a big deficit and a hard pull. Cool, humid, still days mean a gentle one. This is why the same field can need double the water in a heat wave.

Now the soil side. Water in soil isn't a full tank you draw down evenly. Three landmarks matter:

- **Saturation** — every pore is full of water, and none is full of air. Roots need oxygen too, so this is a countdown clock, not a good state.
- **Field capacity** — gravity has drained the big pores (usually a day or two after a soaking rain), water remains in the small ones, and air is back. This is the ideal.
- **Permanent wilting point** — the remaining water clings to soil particles more tightly than roots can pull. There's still water down there; the plant just can't get it.

The usable range between field capacity and wilting point is **plant-available water**. Sandy soil has big pores that drain fast and holds maybe an inch of it per foot of depth. Silt loam holds two or more. That single number explains why a Nebraska sand hill needs frequent light irrigation while an Illinois silt loam can coast for a week.

When available water runs low, the plant hits **water stress**. Its first defense is to close stomata — which stops water loss but also stops CO2 intake, so growth pauses. Push further and leaves roll, wilt, and drop. Timing matters more than total: stress during flowering and pollination costs far more yield than the same stress during early vegetative growth. In corn, a few dry days at silking can cut yield by a third.

The opposite failure is just as real. **Waterlogging** fills every pore, roots suffocate, and in warm soil they can die in 48 to 72 hours. This is why **drainage** — surface grading, or buried perforated pipe called **tile drainage** — is a form of water management every bit as important as irrigation. Much of the American Midwest is farmable only because it was tiled.

So how do we deliver water? Three broad families, in rough order of efficiency:

- **Surface (flood/furrow) irrigation** — water runs down the field by gravity. Cheap, ancient, no energy cost, but typically only 40 to 60% of applied water reaches the root zone. The rest runs off or percolates past the roots.
- **Sprinkler irrigation** — pressurized, sprayed from above. The center pivot, those green circles you see from an airplane over Kansas, is the dominant form. Roughly 70 to 90% efficient; low-pressure drop nozzles near the ground beat high-pressure guns because less spray evaporates in flight.
- **Drip / micro-irrigation** — emitters release water slowly right at the base of each plant. 85 to 95% efficient, allows fertilizer to be delivered in the water (**fertigation**), and keeps foliage dry, which suppresses some diseases. The catch is upfront cost and clogged emitters if the water isn't filtered.

Deciding *when* to irrigate uses one of two logics. **Soil-based**: put sensors in the ground and water when moisture drops past a threshold. **Weather-based**: run a checkbook. Estimate how much water left the field as **evapotranspiration** (ET — transpiration from plants plus evaporation from soil), subtract rain, and refill the deficit. In plain terms:

```
soil water today = soil water yesterday + rain + irrigation - ET - drainage - runoff
```

Public ET networks publish daily numbers for exactly this purpose, and a crop coefficient scales the reference figure to whatever you're growing at whatever growth stage.

One more idea worth knowing: **deficit irrigation**. Sometimes deliberately under-watering during a stage where the crop is insensitive saves a lot of water for a small yield hit — and in wine grapes, mild stress actually improves fruit quality by concentrating sugars and flavor compounds. More water is not always better.

## In Everyday Life

Fly into Denver or Wichita on a clear afternoon and look down. The ground is a quilt of perfect green circles, each about half a mile across, packed inside square fields. Those are center pivots — a quarter-mile arm of sprinklers slowly rotating around a well. The corners stay brown because the arm can't reach them.

Most of those wells tap the Ogallala Aquifer, the vast groundwater layer under the High Plains. It's a useful lesson in the economics of irrigation. In parts of western Kansas the water table has dropped by more than 100 feet since large-scale pumping began, and pumping from deeper costs more diesel or electricity every year. That rising cost is why farmers there swapped high-pressure guns for low-drop nozzles, then added soil moisture probes, and in some counties voluntarily agreed to pump less. Efficiency stopped being an environmental slogan and became a line item.

Meanwhile in California's Central Valley — which grows most of the almonds, pistachios, and processing tomatoes in the U.S. — the story went the other way. Permanent tree and vine crops can't be fallowed in a dry year the way an annual row crop can; you either water the orchard or lose a 20-year investment. That pressure pushed the valley heavily toward drip and micro-sprinklers, and toward buried drip lines in tomatoes. Water in that system trades on an open market, sometimes for several hundred dollars an acre-foot in a drought year, which makes every percentage point of efficiency worth real money.

You can watch the same physics in your own yard. Water a lawn at 2 p.m. in August and a meaningful share evaporates before it lands. Water at 5 a.m. and nearly all of it soaks in — same hose, same minutes, more water in the root zone. And the standard advice to water deeply but less often is soil physics too: a light daily sprinkle wets only the top inch, so roots stay shallow and the plant becomes fragile the moment you skip a day.

## Three-Line Summary

1. Plants must open their stomata to take in CO2, so transpiration — losing water to the air — is an unavoidable cost of photosynthesis, driven by how dry the air is.
2. Usable soil water sits between field capacity and the wilting point; too little causes water stress that hurts most during flowering, and too much suffocates roots, which is why drainage matters as much as irrigation.
3. Irrigation methods run from cheap, leaky flood systems to expensive, precise drip, and scheduling is done either by soil moisture sensors or by an evapotranspiration checkbook that tracks water in versus water out.

## ✅ Self Quiz

**1. Roughly what share of the water a crop absorbs is actually incorporated into the plant's own tissue?**
- A) About 50%
- B) About 20%
- C) Less than 1%
- D) About 90%

**2. O/X: Soil at "field capacity" is the wettest possible state, with every pore space filled with water.**

**3. Which irrigation method is generally the most efficient at delivering water to the root zone?**
- A) Furrow (surface) irrigation
- B) High-pressure sprinkler guns
- C) Drip / micro-irrigation
- D) Flood irrigation

## 📚 Today's Terms

- **Transpiration** — Water evaporating out of a plant's leaves through the stomata; the unavoidable cost of opening pores to absorb CO2.
- **Stomata** — Adjustable microscopic pores on leaf surfaces that let CO2 in and water vapor out; the plant closes them under stress.
- **Field capacity** — The moisture a soil holds after gravity has drained the large pores, leaving both water and air available to roots; the target condition.
- **Permanent wilting point** — The moisture level at which remaining soil water is held too tightly for roots to extract, and the plant cannot recover.
- **Evapotranspiration (ET)** — Combined water loss from plant transpiration and soil surface evaporation; the "withdrawal" figure in irrigation scheduling.
- **Tile drainage** — Perforated pipe buried below the root zone to carry away excess water and prevent roots from suffocating in saturated soil.

---

*Answers: 1 — C. Well over 99% of absorbed water passes through and transpires away; only a tiny fraction ends up as plant tissue. That's the trade a plant makes to get CO2 for photosynthesis. 2 — X (False). The wettest state is saturation, where every pore is water-filled and roots have no oxygen. Field capacity is what remains after gravity drains the large pores, and it's the desirable condition precisely because water and air are both present. 3 — C. Drip and micro-irrigation deliver water directly at the plant base and typically reach 85 to 95% efficiency, versus roughly 40 to 60% for surface methods. The trade-off is high installation cost and the need for clean, filtered water to avoid clogged emitters.*
